title: US Inflation Cools to 3.4% in July, Easing Pressure on the Fed
excerpt: Consumer prices decelerated for a second straight month as core inflation hit its lowest level since February, giving markets a modest lift alongside strong AI earnings.
body:
• July CPI came in at 3.4% year-over-year, matching consensus and decelerating from 3.5% in June
  • Core CPI fell to 2.5%, its lowest reading since February, easing fears of a September rate hike
  • The S&P 500 and Nasdaq closed up 0.3% and 0.5% respectively, buoyed by strong AI earnings from CoreWeave and Super Micro
  • Traders now price a 40% chance the Fed raises rates in September, down from 48% a day earlier

US consumer prices rose 3.4% in the 12 months through July, matching economists' forecasts and easing from June's 3.5% reading, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Wednesday. The in-line print gave Wall Street a measure of relief after two sessions of declines heading into the data.

Core Inflation Hits Five-Month Low

The more closely watched core CPI — which strips out volatile food and energy costs — increased 2.5% year-over-year, down from 2.6% in June and its lowest level since February. Both headline and core readings landed squarely on consensus forecasts compiled by FactSet.

The deceleration extends a cooling trend that began with June's report, which showed headline inflation dropping 0.4% month-over-month — the largest monthly decline since 2020 — driven partly by falling energy prices and a notable slowdown in shelter costs, which rose just 0.1% against a typical 0.3% pace.

Markets Close Higher on AI Momentum

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite rose 0.5% on the day, while the benchmark S&P 500 gained 0.3%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average finished fractionally lower. Much of the session's momentum preceded the CPI release, fueled by strong quarterly earnings from AI-linked companies.

Cloud infrastructure firm CoreWeave, optical networking maker Lumentum, and server manufacturer Super Micro Computer all topped analysts' estimates, reigniting confidence in AI-driven capital spending after a stretch of market uncertainty about the durability of the trade.

"We've seen fresh equity gains overnight, as the latest earnings from CoreWeave and Super Micro Computer led to renewed optimism on the AI trade."

— Henry Allen, Macro Strategist, Deutsche Bank

The 10-year Treasury yield settled around 4.69% at the close, down one basis point from Tuesday, as bond markets digested the inflation data alongside a still-tight labor market backdrop.

Rate Hike Odds Ease

The inflation reading nudged rate expectations lower. According to CME Group's FedWatch tool, traders now see a roughly 40% probability the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates at its mid-September meeting, down from 48% a day earlier. Friday's weaker-than-expected July employment report — which showed the US economy unexpectedly losing jobs — had already begun pulling those odds down.

At its July meeting, the Fed held rates steady, though three of 12 policymakers dissented in favor of a hike. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, who succeeded Jerome Powell two months ago, has maintained a data-dependent posture, pledging to let the numbers guide policy rather than committing to a predetermined path.

"CPI coming down the last couple of months may be enough to prevent the Fed from hiking rates this year. Should CPI snap back higher, then I would expect stocks to sell off on that news."

— Dominic Pappalardo, Chief Multi-Asset Strategist, Morningstar Wealth

Oil Remains the Wildcard

Despite the encouraging inflation print, energy prices remain a source of uncertainty. The ongoing US-Iran conflict has kept crude volatile — Brent crude topped $86 a barrel in mid-July after military strikes near the Strait of Hormuz, before pulling back below $80 this week.

Any sustained rise in oil prices could reverse the disinflationary momentum that has given Warsh room to hold. Investors will look to the producer price index and upcoming retail sales data for further signals on whether the July cooling extends into the broader economy.
